question: When an AI helps solve a famous problem, how should we share the credit between people and machines?
reflection: If machines help us find answers faster, our shared rules for checking and crediting work become even more valuable.

sources.subject: AI is changing what happens after a breach
OpenAI's 10,000 agents solved a 90-year math problem in 88hrs

one_line: AI is reportedly producing real scientific results, which forces new questions about credit, trust and what happens when stolen data meets powerful tools.

top_stories.title: OpenAI agents reportedly crack a famous fluid equation problem
top_stories.what: OpenAI says 10,000 agents on an unreleased model showed in 88 hours that the Navier-Stokes equations can break down, with the proof checked in Lean, while an NYU mathematician disputes how credit was handled.
top_stories.why: Research bodies will need clear rules on who gets credit and who is responsible when AI contributes to discovery.

top_stories.title: Why people still hesitate to hand tasks to agents
top_stories.what: A Forward Future essay argues that most adults now use chatbots, but agents ask for much more: account access, permissions, supervision and trust.
top_stories.why: The barrier is delegation and trust, not awareness, which is a behavioural design problem for any digital service adding agents.

top_stories.title: AI makes stolen data more dangerous
top_stories.what: US reports allege Chinese hackers used AI to search and sort data taken in a breach, turning a large dump into targeted intelligence.
top_stories.why: Agencies that hold personal records should collect less, limit access and plan for faster misuse after any breach.

idea.title: Delegation readiness study
idea.pitch: Measure what makes citizens willing to let an AI agent complete a government task for them, such as booking or renewing a document.
idea.first_step: Draft three task scenarios with different permission levels and test them with ten users in short interviews.

idea_kids.title: Proof detectives
idea_kids.pitch: A puzzle workshop where children check each step of a short logic chain and mark which step is weak, learning that answers need reasons.
idea_kids.first_step: Write six simple logic chains, two of them with one hidden faulty step.
